headline: Walters sees Australia's labour market and minimum wage growth as key supports for ongoing consumer spending
reasoning: Walters notes the minimum wage rose nearly 5% in July, flowing through not only to the lowest-paid workers but also to those on awards — roughly another quarter of the workforce. He emphasises that most Australians who want a job have one, and that while underemployment is drifting up slightly, the labour market remains solid. He argues that as long as the labour market holds, consumers will continue to spend even amid headwinds from interest rates and global uncertainty.
quote: I think it's really positive. Like we saw the minimum wage go up only last month by nearly 5%. And that flows through not just to the the very lowest workers in the economy, but also those that are working on awards. So that's another quarter of the workforce, so they've still got jobs. Most people actually say who want a job, have a job, they might want to work more hours. So we are seeing those underemployment indicators sort of track up a little bit, but it's still a really solid labor market. And the bottom line is, even if you're feeling a bit downbeat and you're worried about interest rates going up and you are paying more on your mortgage if you have one. Remember, only a third of Australians have a mortgage, so the remaining third owner owns their house outright.

headline: Australian household spending proving far more resilient than expected despite three RBA rate hikes and weak sentiment, driven by a solid labour market
reasoning: Walters highlights that the household spending indicator rose 0.8% in June alone despite three rate hikes in 2023, a sharp fall in sentiment post-budget to near-recession levels, and weakness in the housing market. He attributes the resilience to a still-solid labour market, with unemployment hovering around 4–4.5% and strong job growth. He notes the largest driver was transport/petrol spending, which he flags as less encouraging, but takes the headline number as genuinely solid.
quote: Yeah. Way more. I mean, we saw those numbers yesterday. This is the household spending indicator was up 0.8% on the month just in June alone. Remember we've had three rate hikes this year. We've had since the budget some pretty weak outcomes in the housing market and sentiment. We know even though it's improved a little bit in the last couple of months, it fell really sharply after the budget down to levels we've normally seen in recession. So despite all that, we had this really strong consumer spending number. So I think the explanation is probably that the labor market is still in pretty good shape.

However, he emphasises that these corrections are typically short-lived (12–18 months) and that the long-term trend remains strongly upward. He flags a small risk of negative equity for recent buyers who used the government's 5% deposit scheme, but considers this a minor portion of the overall homeowner cohort.

headline: Stephen Walters expects unemployment rate to continue drifting up toward mid-4% range with decent near-term jobs growth masking the trend
reasoning: Walters anticipates a decent employment gain in the June jobs print but flags the unemployment rate as the key metric to watch. The unemployment rate has risen from a trough of ~3.5% a couple of years ago to around 4.6%, and Walters expects it to continue drifting higher. Leading indicators for employment have been weakening. However, strong demand in the publicly-funded care economy continues to support headline jobs growth. He does not expect unemployment to reach 5% soon but sees the trend as upward over a one-year horizon.
quote: I think you'll get a decent gain in employment tomorrow. This will be for the June month. So I think it'll be a decent number. But I think the key one to watch is the unemployment rate. And that's been drifting up. We bottomed out at sort of just about 3.5%. A couple of years ago, and here we are at about 4.6 or thereabouts. So I think you'll get something similar tomorrow. So again, the labor market has been okay. Some of the leading indicators have been weakening, but we're still getting decent jobs. Growth people are still hiring. Firms are still hiring out there. That's still all the demand for for people to work in the care economy that's very heavily public funded. So there's still lots of jobs growth there. So I think you'll still get decent numbers. But for me the one to watch is the jobless rate. And I think that'll continue to drift up.

headline: Stephen Walters sees Australian house prices declining 5–10% as auction clearance rates below 50% signal sustained buyer-seller mismatch
reasoning: Walters argues that budget policies are intentionally designed to bring house prices down, though government ministers won't admit it publicly. He uses auction clearance rates as a leading indicator, noting they have been below 50% for about five weeks, which is historically consistent with falling prices. Most economists expect a fall of 5–10% in this down cycle, which he views as welcome for affordability but notes the market remains extremely expensive in absolute terms.
quote: I think probably auction clearance rates are a good balance in terms of what's going on in the market. They tell you where there's a mismatch between buyers and sellers, and that typically means prices have to come down. So when you get auction clearance rates like we have at the moment that are below 50%, and albeit they bounced above 52 weeks ago and now they're back below 50, it's been about five weeks now that auction clearance rates are below 50. That's really consistent with house prices going down. So yes, that improves affordability very much. At the margin, we've had decades of really strong house price growth. Getting a fall of probably between 5 and 10% is what most economists expect in this little down cycle is welcomed by people who are trying to buy a home, but really, it's still an extremely expensive housing market, just slightly less expensive than it was a few weeks ago.

headline: Stephen Walters expects RBA on hold in August but still sees rate hike later in 2024 as inflation remains above target and accelerating
reasoning: Walters disagrees with the UBS call for an August hike, arguing weakness in the housing market post-budget will keep the RBA on hold for now. However, his core view is that inflation will ultimately override growth weakness and force a hike later in the year. Core inflation is not only above target but accelerating, and new inflationary pressures are emerging from Middle East tensions, with oil prices up 25% in two weeks, which will feed through to petrol prices. The RBA faces a difficult balance between a weakening housing market and worsening inflation.
quote: I still think interest rates will go up. I just don't think it'll be as soon as August. I think we're probably looking at probably the next meeting or sometime later in the year, because I think there's a bit of nervousness in the reserve Bank about what's going on in the housing market post the budget measures. The anecdotes are really pretty awful, frankly. The Da has not yet really caught up with that except auction clearance rates. So that I think is enough to probably keep them on hold. But my big concern is inflation is still above target here. Core inflation is not only above target, it's accelerating away from the target. And we've now got all this new inflation pressure coming through from what's going on in the Middle East. With the strait closed again oil prices up 25% in two weeks. We all know what that means for petrol prices.

headline: Stephen Walters sees Australian economy growing but underperforming potential, held back by weak investment and productivity
reasoning: Walters notes the latest GDP print showed ~2.5% growth, which he describes as okay but below potential. He highlights commentary from Phil Lowe and Bill Kelty lamenting falling living standards, lack of investment and weak productivity as core structural problems. Consumer and business confidence are both at very low levels despite a small bounce. The overall picture is one of an economy doing okay but underwhelming.
quote: Look that was interesting. It's a good sort of overall mix of where the bits and pieces of the economy are fitting together. And I think you've seen some of the commentary this week from people like Phil Lowe, our former reserve Bank governor, and Bill Kelty, former head of the ACTU, not normally on the same page all the time, both lamenting the fall in living standards in Australia and how the economy lacks investment, lacks productivity. And I think that's the core problem, is that we're still doing okay. Like the last GDP numbers we got in June showed the economy growing at about 2.5% at. That's okay. Probably below what we're we're capable of doing, but just sort of struggling a little bit, I think.

headline: Stephen Walters warns against heavy-handed AI regulation in Australia, arguing productivity gains from AI are critical given the worst decade for productivity in 60 years
reasoning: Walters describes Australia's productivity performance as 'truly awful' — the worst decade in 60 years — and sees AI as the key potential remedy. He is concerned that the government's newly announced AI regulatory regime could stifle these gains, drawing a parallel to the heavy-handed European approach. With no serious tax or budget reform on the horizon, he argues AI is potentially Australia's best hope for lifting living standards and urges a light-touch regulatory framework.
quote: It's truly awful. And, uh, the worst decade in 60 years. It's been well documented that our living standards are falling, productivity is is woeful, and AI really learns is what I think is the golden goose here to to get us out of this productivity pickle. Uh, I'm a little concerned that last week, the prime minister announced a regulatory regime for AI. Uh, yes. It does probably need some some guardrails about usage and what you can do with AI. And the unions are very worried about what it means for jobs, and that's understandable. But I really hope we don't take a heavy handed approach here like the Europeans did, because we really need a few golden geese coming our way because we're not getting any serious reform. We're not getting tax reform. Those budget changes, we're not reform, though it does tax increases. So we really need to see some serious reform in the economy in its absence. Maybe AI will be our great savior. So let's not regulate the heck out of it and make those gains much lower than they should be.

headline: Stephen Walters flags Middle East disruption pushing oil prices up 25% in two weeks as a significant new inflation risk for Australia
reasoning: Walters highlights that the closure of the strait and associated Middle East tensions have driven oil prices up approximately 25% in just two weeks. He notes this will have a direct and well-understood pass-through to petrol prices, adding to existing inflationary pressures in Australia. This compounds the already challenging inflation environment where core CPI is above target and accelerating.
quote: We've now got all this new inflation pressure coming through from what's going on in the Middle East. With the strait closed again oil prices up 25% in two weeks. We all know what that means for petrol prices. So I think the Reserve Bank's got a difficult balance here.

headline: Australia's unemployment rate expected to drift gradually higher toward 5% over the next year, with AI disruption a contributing factor
reasoning: Stephen Walters notes that while the Australian labour market remains decent with firms still hiring, particularly in the publicly-funded care economy, leading indicators are weakening. He expects the jobless rate to drift up from around 4.6%, moving through the mid-four percent range before potentially rising above 5% in a year's time. He attributes part of the disruption to AI's impact on the workforce.
quote: I think you'll still get decent numbers. But for me the one to watch is the jobless rate. And I think that'll continue to drift up. I don't think we're getting like a 5% unemployment rate anytime soon. I think you'll get sort of four sixes and four fives and four seven seconds or thereabouts. But I think over time, if you ask me again, in a year's time we might be above 5%.
